Statistics can make this subject strangely hygienic. Percentages, surveys, victimization rates. So let me make one thing less abstract at the outset.
When I say violence against women, I am talking about women _including me._
I will leave it there. Women are routinely asked to produce our wounds before anyone will let us discuss the weapon, and I'm not interested.
My argument begins at Cornell University.
A former student, identified in court as Jane Doe, has filed a civil lawsuit alleging that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. The complaint includes screenshots of a group chat message to fraternity members graphically suggesting that a woman upstairs was sexually available. The defendants dispute the allegations. Cornell says its investigation resulted in expulsions and suspensions and that the fraternity chapter was barred from campus. The Tompkins County district attorney, who initially declined to bring charges and has identified discrepancies between Doe's original police statement and her civil complaint, has reopened the criminal investigation and intends to present the case to a grand jury. Doe's attorney disputes the adequacy of the original investigation. These are serious questions for investigators and, potentially, jurors to resolve. [CBS News](https://substack.com/redirect/500bf808-8ed9-4293-bf78-068213af23d5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The evidence has to be examined carefully. _So does the social setting the complaint describes._ A group chat is a way of summoning people, establishing a shared understanding, and testing what others will allow. If the allegations are established, the danger was not confined to what happened behind one door. It extended into the relationships surrounding that room.
**How many people does it take to make one rape possible?**
I do not mean how many people physically participate. I mean how many people must accept the conditions around it.
_Who sees someone profoundly intoxicated and decides their vulnerability invites exploitation? Who turns that vulnerability into a joke or an invitation? Who hears a friend describe what he intends to do and decides that friendship requires silence? Who has authority afterward to investigate, protect, discipline, or prosecute, and uses it well -- or poorly?_
Those responsibilities are different. A person who commits an assault is responsible for the assault. A friend who could safely intervene and chooses not to bears a different responsibility. An institution that mishandles evidence has obligations of its own.
Moral seriousness requires us to distinguish them. It also requires us to stop treating every failure short of perpetration as nothing.
Somewhere nearby is the familiar answer: _Well,**I** didn't rape anybody._
I believe you. But **that was not the question.**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/932ebdd0-2362-43c8-ab93-8f09a69f9ce6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

## What a group permits
"Not all men" is true. Criminal guilt is individual. An accusation requires evidence, and an innocent person must not be punished because the allegation is horrifying. Fair process protects people from the power of institutions that can get things wrong.
But "not all men" is often offered as the end of a conversation that has barely begun. Not all men rape. The actual next question should be: _What do men who do not rape do ... when the man who does is their friend?_
Predators do not need universal male approval. They need enough people nearby who will give them access, silence, excuses, or the benefit of a doubt that somehow never reaches the woman. A fraternity could contain many men who would never assault anyone and still be dangerous if none of them will cross a brother. A workplace can prohibit harassment in writing while everyone knows that reporting a valuable employee will cost the complainant more than it costs the perpetrator.
There is research behind the intuition that group norms can change conduct of their members. A longitudinal study of college men found an association between fraternity membership and later sexual aggression even after accounting for earlier aggression. Its authors examined both **selection** , meaning who joins, and **socialization** , meaning what membership may subsequently encourage. That does not establish that every fraternity has the same culture or that membership causes any particular assault. It does tell us to **look inside the group,** rather than treating it as scenery. [PMC](https://substack.com/redirect/ea89ed75-21e4-4074-befd-eea25eb814de?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Anthropologist Peggy Reeves Sanday spent decades examining how sexual violence relates to status, gender, and social organization, including within American fraternities. Her terms "rape prone" and "rape free" can sound more absolute than real communities ever are. Their useful insight is that cultures vary in what they reward and restrain, and those variations produce real consequences in different outcomes. The variation can exist within one country, one university, even among houses on the same campus. There is no single American male culture whose effects we must helplessly accept. [PMC](https://substack.com/redirect/ea89ed75-21e4-4074-befd-eea25eb814de?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
That is one place to start looking for an alternative: where men have status because they exercise restraint, where a woman's visible incapacity ends the party rather than starting a group chat, and where loyalty to a friend does not include helping him harm someone.
Such a healthy masculine group is developed through decisions its members make when an aroused male friend is present, and the woman has less power.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9tZWxpc3NhNGNvbmdyZXNzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.6xB8iHgwU3kYHd6WC_58TxNUEYZI9VFtnoG7Z80oNGI?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=218052633)
## What looks sexual
There is another question beneath the question of intervention. **Why would an incapacitated woman look like a sexual opportunity at all?**
A person who cannot understand what is happening, cannot meaningfully participate, or becomes frightened or unresponsive should call forth **concern**. Stop. Check in on her. Get her water. Find her friend. Help her get somewhere safe. Seek medical help if she needs it.
In healthy sex, another person's desire is a deep, integral, and enjoyable part of the experience. Their pleasure and consent is not an obstacle to your access to their body -- they are who you are having sex _**with.**_
Yet coercion, humiliation, incapacitation, and female pain have all been made into sexual material. This predates internet pornography in Western culture by a few thousand years or so. Neither can the evidence support the tidy assertion that pornography alone creates rapists. Content, prior beliefs, age, and social setting matter.
Still, boys may encounter repeated depictions of women as bodies to use years before they have experienced a real sexual relationship. Modeling shapes how they approach those early encounters. Were the women in those porn videos humanized and treated with passionate, attentive kindness? If you, like me, shrug and smirk sadly at the mere suggestion, that tells us plenty.
Growing boys often also encounter men offering **contempt for women** as advice about masculinity. The cultural question is what these lessons make familiar -- and what other adults in their lives do to challenge them, and whether that happens **in time.**
Consider the difference between the word _rape_ and phrases that conceal the conduct: _getting her upstairs_ , _taking a chance_ , _she was out of it_ , _things got carried away_.
A young man can understand that rape is condemned and still be surrounded by language that helps him avoid recognizing coercion when he or his friends commit it. The group can then discuss his intentions, her drinking, or the damage to his future... without fully naming what happened to her.
None of this requires a theory that men are born defective, and I reject that theory completely. **Men are extraordinarily capable of gentleness, restraint, courage, kindness, and care.**
That is why teaching and expectations among peers and role models matter so much. If these qualities were absent or impossible, then asking men to step up, show up, intervene, and **protect her** would make little sense.

## Who pays?
There is a way to measure some of sexual violence's reach beyond police reports. Look at the invoice. How much does avoiding men's violence actually cost women -- financially, in lost time, in divided attention, in lack of trust or stability?
The rideshare instead of the walk home. The more expensive apartment near transit and light. The location sharing, the drink cover, the alarm, the friend asked to accompany you. The job declined because the shift ends after dark. The mental work of calculating exits and watching for the man who is watching you.
Many women make these calculations before anything has happened to them at night. Some make them because something has.
We call these measures "safety precautions," as if they were a collection of personal preferences. Much of the time they are **privately purchased adaptations to a public failure.** The costs fall on women in money, time, attention, movement, and ease. The people creating the risk almost never receive the bill.
A similar transfer of consequence occurs after an assault. A woman may leave a campus, lose a semester, struggle to sleep, distrust friends, change the places she goes or the relationships she can bear to enter. She may carry these profoundly damaging consequences for decades. Yet nobody seems to care about these impacts to a life already underway.
When a young man is accused, questions about evidence and fair process are - yes - necessary. What if the allegation is mistaken? What standard should an institution use? How can it investigate without prejudging either person? A just society has to answer those questions.
But even after wrongdoing is established, public sympathy can remain fixed on **his** interrupted promise. Will he finish his degree? Will he get a job? Must one mistake define his life? Speaking as a woman, the perpetual focus on _his_ feelings, _his_ future, when _he_ committed the crime in question, is nauseating. Why shouldn't a criminal suffer consequences? We expect that any other criminal would. **Isn 't rape a crime?**
We should be able to care about proportionate consequences without allowing her future to disappear. **Accountability may alter his life. Good. It should. His sexual violence has already altered hers.**
Fair process establishes -- with evidence -- what happened before imposing consequences; the consequences _themselves_ are not injustice.

## Four ways to arrange responsibility
Americans know our own arrangements well enough that we sometimes mistake them for the only available ones. We prohibit rape, assign criminal investigations to police and prosecutors, leave universities and employers to conduct their own proceedings, and expect individuals to manage much of their daily safety. Other societies and legal traditions have organized these responsibilities differently. Understanding those differences requires looking at what each system actually does, rather than choosing a country with a frightening penalty and assuming it has solved sexual violence.
**China places considerable emphasis on severe criminal punishment and restrictions on access to children.** Its criminal law provides a baseline sentence of three to ten years for rape, with aggravated cases potentially punishable by longer imprisonment, life imprisonment, or death. Aggravating circumstances include gang rape, multiple victims, serious injury or death, and certain offenses against young children. China also has screening and occupational-exclusion systems intended to keep people with specified histories of abuse away from work involving minors. Those restrictions address a practical question that a prison sentence alone cannot answer: who should be allowed to return to a position that gives them access to vulnerable people?
But the severity of the law does not establish how consistently it operates. A UNFPA-supported study of one county in central China found substantial self-reported sexual violence, and approximately three quarters of the men who admitted rape reported experiencing no legal consequences. The study was not nationally representative, so its findings cannot be projected onto the entire country. They nevertheless make it impossible to treat low police-recorded rape figures as proof that sexual violence is vanishingly rare. [china.unfpa.org](https://substack.com/redirect/eecbee7e-8a44-48d5-b941-7781bc407e9c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
China therefore illustrates both a possible protective measure and an enforcement failure. Excluding people convicted of abuse from child-facing work can reduce access to potential victims. Threatening an extreme punishment does little to restrain someone who expects never to be investigated or convicted. The operative question is what happens between the assault and the courtroom: whether a victim can report safely, whether evidence is gathered, and whether authorities pursue the case.
**Classical Islamic fiqh places sexual violation within a much broader account of rights, duties, coercion, and justice.** Americans have often encountered Islamic law through images of corporal punishment, with little explanation of the legal and moral system surrounding it. _Shari 'ah_ refers to the normative religious framework; _fiqh_ is the human jurisprudence developed through interpretation. It encompasses worship, contracts, property, inheritance, charity, family obligations, commercial conduct, and duties toward other people. The fixed punishments known as _hudud_ occupy one part of that larger tradition. They are not a complete description of what Islamic law is for.
Within that criminal jurisprudence, some jurists evaluated rape through the law of _zina_ , prohibited sexual intercourse outside a lawful relationship, while distinguishing sharply between the perpetrator and the person coerced. Coercion removed the victim's culpability. The fact that intercourse had occurred did not make a raped woman a consenting participant or mean she should receive the punishment prescribed for voluntary illicit sex. Her lack of consent was a legal fact with consequences for responsibility.
That principle is especially important because Americans sometimes hear that a woman must produce four eyewitnesses to a rape or be punished herself. That collapses several different legal questions into one. The demanding witness rules associated with a fixed _zina_ punishment concerned whether that particular punishment could be imposed; they were not a universal rule governing every possible finding of rape, every remedy, or the victim's exemption from culpability. Schools differed over evidence, presumptions, compensation, and other forms of punishment. A failure to establish the conditions for a _hadd_ , the singular of _hudud_ , did not by itself establish that a complainant had voluntarily committed _zina_. Hina Azam's scholarship documents these distinctions and the substantial differences between classical Hanafi and Maliki doctrines. [www.cambridge.org](https://substack.com/redirect/5e518e6c-0362-4bd3-912d-64a1079aef5b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Other jurists approached sexual violation through wrongful appropriation or through _hirabah_ , a category associated with violent predation, terror, and the destruction of public security. The Maliki jurist Ibn al-'Arabi treated rape as an especially grave form of _hirabah_. In that interpretation, the offense was understood as an attack on a person's protected security, with implications for the community's duty to restrain the attacker. _Hirabah_ belongs among the gravest categories of Islamic criminal jurisprudence. Qur'an 5:33 identifies penalties that can include death, with their application depending on the conduct established and the juristic interpretation.
The seriousness of that category should be understood alongside the limits imposed on punishment. Classical jurists developed demanding evidentiary rules for _hudud_ and doctrines directing judges to avoid fixed punishments where legally significant doubt remained. A tradition could therefore regard predation as an enormous wrong while insisting that the sovereign satisfy a high burden before inflicting an irreversible penalty. Depending on the school and legal classification, other remedies could include compensation or discretionary punishment. "Rape always carries the death penalty under Sharia" remains an inaccurate summary, as does the claim that every child rape automatically carries a capital sentence.
There are also failures that must remain visible. Classical jurisprudence generally did not recognize marital rape through the modern principle that consent is required within marriage as well as outside it. Some modern statutes imposed in Islam's name have exposed rape complainants to prosecution for illicit sex, producing outcomes profoundly at odds with protecting a coerced person. Azam's work helps explain how those codifications differ from the complexity of classical doctrines, but the people harmed by them cannot be written out of the comparison. [www.cambridge.org](https://substack.com/redirect/21553263-f29f-4c64-945d-7520593dd2fd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Nor can we infer how effectively centuries of diverse institutions prevented rape merely from the existence of their doctrines. What the tradition gives us is a substantial set of questions: who was coerced, whose rights were violated, what the victim was owed, what could be proved, and what obligations followed for the community and its authorities. A contemporary system can learn from those questions and from the gravity attached to _hirabah_ , while rejecting any rule that leaves a wife without sexual autonomy or turns a complainant's request for protection into a danger to herself.
**Scandinavia offers several contemporary systems built around gender equality, public services, and, increasingly, consent-based criminal law.** Sweden, Denmark, and Norway have distinct laws and institutional histories; they should not be treated as one jurisdiction. The general direction of consent-based reform is to make voluntary participation central to the definition of rape, rather than requiring a victim to demonstrate that an attacker used a particular degree of force. Alongside criminal law, these countries use public institutions to investigate violence, provide care, and study its prevalence.
These arrangements broaden what government recognizes as its responsibility. They can give victims routes to healthcare and assistance that do not depend entirely on privately purchasing protection. They also allow a society to ask whether sexual violence persists even when it officially endorses equality. Norwegian national research reports substantial lifetime sexual victimization, including abuse beginning in childhood. Public commitment to equality has not eliminated sexual coercion in private relationships. [www.nkvts.no](https://substack.com/redirect/68e68866-c62d-4f69-84bc-591fca699281?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Nor should national police statistics be read as a simple league table of safety. A broader legal definition, greater willingness to disclose, or different recording practices can produce more recorded offenses without a corresponding increase in underlying violence. To judge whether reforms work, we need evidence about victimization, reporting, investigations, outcomes, and access to care. Scandinavia supplies institutional choices worth examining, rather than proof that an egalitarian reputation makes women safe.
**The United States distributes responsibility across criminal courts, civil proceedings, institutions, and individuals, with substantial variation among states and communities.** Criminal prosecution requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Universities and employers can investigate misconduct under separate rules and standards, and civil litigation provides another possible route to a remedy. These processes serve different purposes, but a victim may have to navigate several of them while also managing the immediate effects on her health, housing, education, or employment.
The country also contains sharply different local cultures beneath its broad public condemnation of rape. Research on fraternities examines both selection, meaning the characteristics of men who join, and socialization, meaning what the group subsequently encourages. A longitudinal study found an association between fraternity membership and later sexual aggression after accounting for earlier aggression. Other research identifies high-risk alcohol use as an important part of the association. These findings establish neither the guilt of an individual member nor identical conditions in every fraternity. They identify settings in which prevention must address access, drinking practices, status, and peer expectations together. [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://substack.com/redirect/ea89ed75-21e4-4074-befd-eea25eb814de?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The variation within the United States is especially revealing. People can live under the same criminal law while belonging to groups with very different expectations about intervention. In one group, a man who exploits an incapacitated woman may expect protection. In another, he may expect his friends to stop him, preserve evidence, and tell the truth. The statute is the same. His anticipated freedom to act is not.
Taken together, these comparisons give us a more useful set of questions than "Who punishes rapists hardest?" Does the law recognize the violation? Can the person harmed seek help safely? Will someone investigate competently? What consequences follow a supported finding? Who provides care and restitution? What keeps a person who has abused others from regaining access to vulnerable people? And what do friends, families, and institutions do before a case ever reaches the state?
A society may answer one of those questions well and fail another. Severe punishment can coexist with impunity. Religious concern for coercion can coexist with exclusions that leave some victims unprotected. Public investment in equality can coexist with persistent private abuse. Formal condemnation can coexist with a fraternity's quiet permission.
Those failures are reasons to examine the machinery more closely. They are also evidence that our present arrangements are choices people can change.

## What we could choose
**We could begin earlier than college orientation.** Children can learn that another person's body and wishes are real, that affection does not create entitlement, and that courage includes refusing a friend's cruelty. Young people deserve honest education about desire, intoxication, coercion, and the difference between mutual sex and obtaining access to someone unable to choose.
**We could make intervention a practiced social skill.** A friend can interrupt, call for help, bring in another person, or leave with someone in danger. Institutions can train people to recognize the moment when awkwardness becomes a poor excuse for inaction. Research reviews suggest bystander programs can improve willingness and capacity to intervene, though training alone cannot bear the full weight of prevention. [PubMed](https://substack.com/redirect/1d60858d-8e9e-4f17-bd40-495f587dd347?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
**We could build investigative systems** that preserve evidence, communicate clearly across campus and criminal processes, protect complainants from retaliation, and give accused people a fair chance to answer the evidence against them. We could keep people found responsible for sexual abuse away from positions that give them access to vulnerable people. We could ask institutions to account for what happens to a student's education after an assault with at least the care they devote to the accused student's prospects.
**And men could make a different kind of loyalty ordinary.** The man who sees his friend steering an incapacitated woman upstairs can follow and intervene. The man who hears coercion described as conquest can name it and shame it. The man who learns credible facts about someone he loves can help establish the truth without organizing everyone else to protect that person's standing. None of this demands that he pronounce guilt before an investigation. It asks him to take another person's safety seriously before the opportunity to help has passed.
**I think about the men I want my son to know.** I want him surrounded by men who understand that _**their care has to do something in the world.**_ That their courage and their capability should count for something. That their integrity is consequential. They should be able to enjoy friendship without surrendering judgment to it, and to tell the truth about a friend even when doing so hurts.
**Sexual violence does not require "every man".** It requires perpetrators and opportunities, often aided by people and institutions that decide stopping the harm belongs to somebody else. We have built many of those arrangements ourselves. The differences between communities, traditions, and countries tell us that people can build differently.
* * *
So yes, not all men. I believe that. I **am asking what responsibility belongs to the rest of you** -- and if you, yourself, do not commit rape, would never commit rape... -- _what are you doing to make rape costly to the men you know who do?_
And if you, a man, are **sure** you don't know any men who've abused women, consider this -- that **every woman I have ever known, including myself, has experienced sexual assault or abuse by a man.**
How is it possible that both can be true?
I'll leave you with that.

So let me make one thing less abstract at the outset. When I say violence against women, I am talking about women including me. I will leave it there. Women are routinely asked to produce our wounds before anyone will let us discuss the weapon, and I'm not interested. My argument begins at Cornell University. A former student, identified in court as Jane Doe, has filed a civil lawsuit alleging that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. The complaint includes screenshots of a group chat message to fraternity members graphically suggesting that a woman upstairs was sexually available. The defendants dispute the allegations. Cornell says its investigation resulted in expulsions and suspensions and that the fraternity chapter was barred from campus. The Tompkins County district attorney, who initially declined to bring charges and has identified discrepancies between Doe's original police statement and her civil complaint, has reopened the criminal investigation and intends to present the case to a grand jury. Doe's attorney disputes the adequacy of the original investigation. These are serious questions for investigators and, potentially, jurors to resolve. The evidence has to be examined carefully. So does the social setting the complaint describes. A group chat is a way of summoning people, establishing a shared understanding, and testing what others will allow. If the allegations are established, the danger was not confined to what happened behind one door. It extended into the relationships surrounding that room. How many people does it take to make one rape possible? I do not mean how many people physically participate. I mean how many people must accept the conditions around it. Who sees someone profoundly intoxicated and decides their vulnerability invites exploitation? Who turns that vulnerability into a joke or an invitation? Who hears a friend describe what he intends to do and decides that friendship requires silence? Who has authority afterward to investigate, protect, discipline, or prosecute, and uses it well -- or poorly? Those responsibilities are different. A person who commits an assault is responsible for the assault. A friend who could safely intervene and chooses not to bears a different responsibility. An institution that mishandles evidence has obligations of its own. Moral seriousness requires us to distinguish them. It also requires us to stop treating every failure short of perpetration as nothing. Somewhere nearby is the familiar answer: Well,I didn't rape anybody. I believe you. But that was not the question. | | ---|---|--- What a group permits "Not all men" is true. Criminal guilt is individual. An accusation requires evidence, and an innocent person must not be punished because the allegation is horrifying. Fair process protects people from the power of institutions that can get things wrong. But "not all men" is often offered as the end of a conversation that has barely begun. Not all men rape. The actual next question should be: What do men who do not rape do ... when the man who does is their friend? Predators do not need universal male approval. They need enough people nearby who will give them access, silence, excuses, or the benefit of a doubt that somehow never reaches the woman. A fraternity could contain many men who would never assault anyone and still be dangerous if none of them will cross a brother. A workplace can prohibit harassment in writing while everyone knows that reporting a valuable employee will cost the complainant more than it costs the perpetrator. There is research behind the intuition that group norms can change conduct of their members. A longitudinal study of college men found an association between fraternity membership and later sexual aggression even after accounting for earlier aggression. Its authors examined both selection , meaning who joins, and socialization , meaning what membership may subsequently encourage. That does not establish that every fraternity has the same culture or that membership causes any particular assault. It does tell us to look inside the group, rather than treating it as scenery. Anthropologist Peggy Reeves Sanday spent decades examining how sexual violence relates to status, gender, and social organization, including within American fraternities. Her terms "rape prone" and "rape free" can sound more absolute than real communities ever are. Their useful insight is that cultures vary in what they reward and restrain, and those variations produce real consequences in different outcomes. The variation can exist within one country, one university, even among houses on the same campus. There is no single American male culture whose effects we must helplessly accept. That is one place to start looking for an alternative: where men have status because they exercise restraint, where a woman's visible incapacity ends the party rather than starting a group chat, and where loyalty to a friend does not include helping him harm someone. Such a healthy masculine group is developed through decisions its members make when an aroused male friend is present, and the woman has less power. What looks sexual There is another question beneath the question of intervention. Why would an incapacitated woman look like a sexual opportunity at all? A person who cannot understand what is happening, cannot meaningfully participate, or becomes frightened or unresponsive should call forth concern. Stop. Check in on her. Get her water. Find her friend. Help her get somewhere safe. Seek medical help if she needs it. In healthy sex, another person's desire is a deep, integral, and enjoyable part of the experience. Their pleasure and consent is not an obstacle to your access to their body -- they are who you are having sex with. Yet coercion, humiliation, incapacitation, and female pain have all been made into sexual material. This predates internet pornography in Western culture by a few thousand years or so. Neither can the evidence support the tidy assertion that pornography alone creates rapists. Content, prior beliefs, age, and social setting matter. Still, boys may encounter repeated depictions of women as bodies to use years before they have experienced a real sexual relationship. Modeling shapes how they approach those early encounters. Were the women in those porn videos humanized and treated with passionate, attentive kindness? If you, like me, shrug and smirk sadly at the mere suggestion, that tells us plenty. Growing boys often also encounter men offering contempt for women as advice about masculinity. The cultural question is what these lessons make familiar -- and what other adults in their lives do to challenge them, and whether that happens in time. A woman may leave a campus, lose a semester, struggle to sleep, distrust friends, change the places she goes or the relationships she can bear to enter. She may carry these profoundly damaging consequences for decades. Yet nobody seems to care about these impacts to a life already underway. When a young man is accused, questions about evidence and fair process are - yes - necessary. What if the allegation is mistaken? What standard should an institution use? How can it investigate without prejudging either person? A just society has to answer those questions. But even after wrongdoing is established, public sympathy can remain fixed on his interrupted promise. Will he finish his degree? Will he get a job? Must one mistake define his life? Speaking as a woman, the perpetual focus on his feelings, his future, when he committed the crime in question, is nauseating. Why shouldn't a criminal suffer consequences? We expect that any other criminal would. Isn 't rape a crime? We should be able to care about proportionate consequences without allowing her future to disappear. Accountability may alter his life. Good. It should. His sexual violence has already altered hers. Fair process establishes -- with evidence -- what happened before imposing consequences; the consequences themselves are not injustice. Four ways to arrange responsibility Americans know our own arrangements well enough that we sometimes mistake them for the only available ones. We prohibit rape, assign criminal investigations to police and prosecutors, leave universities and employers to conduct their own proceedings, and expect individuals to manage much of their daily safety. Other societies and legal traditions have organized these responsibilities differently. Understanding those differences requires looking at what each system actually does, rather than choosing a country with a frightening penalty and assuming it has solved sexual violence. China places considerable emphasis on severe criminal punishment and restrictions on access to children. Its criminal law provides a baseline sentence of three to ten years for rape, with aggravated cases potentially punishable by longer imprisonment, life imprisonment, or death. Aggravating circumstances include gang rape, multiple victims, serious injury or death, and certain offenses against young children. China also has screening and occupational-exclusion systems intended to keep people with specified histories of abuse away from work involving minors. Those restrictions address a practical question that a prison sentence alone cannot answer: who should be allowed to return to a position that gives them access to vulnerable people? But the severity of the law does not establish how consistently it operates. A UNFPA-supported study of one county in central China found substantial self-reported sexual violence, and approximately three quarters of the men who admitted rape reported experiencing no legal consequences. The study was not nationally representative, so its findings cannot be projected onto the entire country. They nevertheless make it impossible to treat low police-recorded rape figures as proof that sexual violence is vanishingly rare. China therefore illustrates both a possible protective measure and an enforcement failure. Excluding people convicted of abuse from child-facing work can reduce access to potential victims. Threatening an extreme punishment does little to restrain someone who expects never to be investigated or convicted. The operative question is what happens between the assault and the courtroom: whether a victim can report safely, whether evidence is gathered, and whether authorities pursue the case. Classical Islamic fiqh places sexual violation within a much broader account of rights, duties, coercion, and justice. Americans have often encountered Islamic law through images of corporal punishment, with little explanation of the legal and moral system surrounding it. Shari 'ah refers to the normative religious framework; fiqh is the human jurisprudence developed through interpretation. It encompasses worship, contracts, property, inheritance, charity, family obligations, commercial conduct, and duties toward other people. The fixed punishments known as hudud occupy one part of that larger tradition. They are not a complete description of what Islamic law is for. Within that criminal jurisprudence, some jurists evaluated rape through the law of zina , prohibited sexual intercourse outside a lawful relationship, while distinguishing sharply between the perpetrator and the person coerced. Coercion removed the victim's culpability. The fact that intercourse had occurred did not make a raped woman a consenting participant or mean she should receive the punishment prescribed for voluntary illicit sex. Her lack of consent was a legal fact with consequences for responsibility. That principle is especially important because Americans sometimes hear that a woman must produce four eyewitnesses to a rape or be punished herself. That collapses several different legal questions into one. The demanding witness rules associated with a fixed zina punishment concerned whether that particular punishment could be imposed; they were not a universal rule governing every possible finding of rape, every remedy, or the victim's exemption from culpability. Schools differed over evidence, presumptions, compensation, and other forms of punishment. A failure to establish the conditions for a hadd , the singular of hudud , did not by itself establish that a complainant had voluntarily committed zina. Hina Azam's scholarship documents these distinctions and the substantial differences between classical Hanafi and Maliki doctrines. Other jurists approached sexual violation through wrongful appropriation or through hirabah , a category associated with violent predation, terror, and the destruction of public security. The Maliki jurist Ibn al-'Arabi treated rape as an especially grave form of hirabah. In that interpretation, the offense was understood as an attack on a person's protected security, with implications for the community's duty to restrain the attacker. Hirabah belongs among the gravest categories of Islamic criminal jurisprudence. Qur'an 5:33 identifies penalties that can include death, with their application depending on the conduct established and the juristic interpretation. The seriousness of that category should be understood alongside the limits imposed on punishment. Classical jurists developed demanding evidentiary rules for hudud and doctrines directing judges to avoid fixed punishments where legally significant doubt remained. A tradition could therefore regard predation as an enormous wrong while insisting that the sovereign satisfy a high burden before inflicting an irreversible penalty. Depending on the school and legal classification, other remedies could include compensation or discretionary punishment. "Rape always carries the death penalty under Sharia" remains an inaccurate summary, as does the claim that every child rape automatically carries a capital sentence. There are also failures that must remain visible. Classical jurisprudence generally did not recognize marital rape through the modern principle that consent is required within marriage as well as outside it. Some modern statutes imposed in Islam's name have exposed rape complainants to prosecution for illicit sex, producing outcomes profoundly at odds with protecting a coerced person. Azam's work helps explain how those codifications differ from the complexity of classical doctrines, but the people harmed by them cannot be written out of the comparison. Nor can we infer how effectively centuries of diverse institutions prevented rape merely from the existence of their doctrines. What the tradition gives us is a substantial set of questions: who was coerced, whose rights were violated, what the victim was owed, what could be proved, and what obligations followed for the community and its authorities. A contemporary system can learn from those questions and from the gravity attached to hirabah , while rejecting any rule that leaves a wife without sexual autonomy or turns a complainant's request for protection into a danger to herself. Scandinavia offers several contemporary systems built around gender equality, public services, and, increasingly, consent-based criminal law. Sweden, Denmark, and Norway have distinct laws and institutional histories; they should not be treated as one jurisdiction. The general direction of consent-based reform is to make voluntary participation central to the definition of rape, rather than requiring a victim to demonstrate that an attacker used a particular degree of force. Alongside criminal law, these countries use public institutions to investigate violence, provide care, and study its prevalence. These arrangements broaden what government recognizes as its responsibility. They can give victims routes to healthcare and assistance that do not depend entirely on privately purchasing protection. They also allow a society to ask whether sexual violence persists even when it officially endorses equality. Norwegian national research reports substantial lifetime sexual victimization, including abuse beginning in childhood. Public commitment to equality has not eliminated sexual coercion in private relationships. Nor should national police statistics be read as a simple league table of safety. A broader legal definition, greater willingness to disclose, or different recording practices can produce more recorded offenses without a corresponding increase in underlying violence. To judge whether reforms work, we need evidence about victimization, reporting, investigations, outcomes, and access to care. Scandinavia supplies institutional choices worth examining, rather than proof that an egalitarian reputation makes women safe. The United States distributes responsibility across criminal courts, civil proceedings, institutions, and individuals, with substantial variation among states and communities. Criminal prosecution requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Universities and employers can investigate misconduct under separate rules and standards, and civil litigation provides another possible route to a remedy. These processes serve different purposes, but a victim may have to navigate several of them while also managing the immediate effects on her health, housing, education, or employment. The country also contains sharply different local cultures beneath its broad public condemnation of rape. Research on fraternities examines both selection, meaning the characteristics of men who join, and socialization, meaning what the group subsequently encourages. A longitudinal study found an association between fraternity membership and later sexual aggression after accounting for earlier aggression. Other research identifies high-risk alcohol use as an important part of the association. These findings establish neither the guilt of an individual member nor identical conditions in every fraternity. They identify settings in which prevention must address access, drinking practices, status, and peer expectations together. The variation within the United States is especially revealing. People can live under the same criminal law while belonging to groups with very different expectations about intervention. In one group, a man who exploits an incapacitated woman may expect protection. In another, he may expect his friends to stop him, preserve evidence, and tell the truth. The statute is the same. His anticipated freedom to act is not. Taken together, these comparisons give us a more useful set of questions than "Who punishes rapists hardest?" Does the law recognize the violation? Can the person harmed seek help safely? Will someone investigate competently? What consequences follow a supported finding? Who provides care and restitution? What keeps a person who has abused others from regaining access to vulnerable people? And what do friends, families, and institutions do before a case ever reaches the state? A society may answer one of those questions well and fail another. Severe punishment can coexist with impunity. Religious concern for coercion can coexist with exclusions that leave some victims unprotected. Public investment in equality can coexist with persistent private abuse. Formal condemnation can coexist with a fraternity's quiet permission. Those failures are reasons to examine the machinery more closely. They are also evidence that our present arrangements are choices people can change. What we could choose We could begin earlier than college orientation. Children can learn that another person's body and wishes are real, that affection does not create entitlement, and that courage includes refusing a friend's cruelty. Young people deserve honest education about desire, intoxication, coercion, and the difference between mutual sex and obtaining access to someone unable to choose. We could make intervention a practiced social skill. A friend can interrupt, call for help, bring in another person, or leave with someone in danger. Institutions can train people to recognize the moment when awkwardness becomes a poor excuse for inaction. Research reviews suggest bystander programs can improve willingness and capacity to intervene, though training alone cannot bear the full weight of prevention. We could build investigative systems that preserve evidence, communicate clearly across campus and criminal processes, protect complainants from retaliation, and give accused people a fair chance to answer the evidence against them. We could keep people found responsible for sexual abuse away from positions that give them access to vulnerable people. We could ask institutions to account for what happens to a student's education after an assault with at least the care they devote to the accused student's prospects. And men could make a different kind of loyalty ordinary. The man who sees his friend steering an incapacitated woman upstairs can follow and intervene. The man who hears coercion described as conquest can name it and shame it. The man who learns credible facts about someone he loves can help establish the truth without organizing everyone else to protect that person's standing. None of this demands that he pronounce guilt before an investigation. It asks him to take another person's safety seriously before the opportunity to help has passed. I think about the men I want my son to know. I want him surrounded by men who understand that their care has to do something in the world. That their courage and their capability should count for something. That their integrity is consequential. They should be able to enjoy friendship without surrendering judgment to it, and to tell the truth about a friend even when doing so hurts. Sexual violence does not require "every man". It requires perpetrators and opportunities, often aided by people and institutions that decide stopping the harm belongs to somebody else. We have built many of those arrangements ourselves. The differences between communities, traditions, and countries tell us that people can build differently. So yes, not all men. I believe that. I am asking what responsibility belongs to the rest of you -- and if you, yourself, do not commit rape, would never commit rape... -- what are you doing to make rape costly to the men you know who do? And if you, a man, are sure you don't know any men who've abused women, consider this -- that every woman I have ever known, including myself, has experienced sexual assault or abuse by a man.** How is it possible that both can be true? I'll leave you with that. You 're currently a free subscriber to "It's a Matter of Integrity" by Melissa Chaudhry. Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows has finally responded to a Feb. 13 Freedom of Access Act request -- 228 days after the simple inquiry was submitted -- revealing that a left-wing NGO funded by George Soros and Arabella Advisers somehow obtained Maine election materials in advance of the 2025 election.
The Maine Wire submitted the Freedom of Access Act request after a Maine resident discovered 250 Maine absentee ballots haphazardly packed into an Amazon Prime package and a delivered to their Newburgh home.
In the following days, Sec. Bellows promised that her office would investigate the "bad actors" responsible for the worst breach in state election security in three decades, but her detectives never interviewed multiple individuals who handled the ballots after they were discovered.
Investigative journalism costs time and money. Please consider supporting The Robinson Report with a subscription.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..yTbNsOrBWrFzPH-RhdDrpbPfgpy0ijcVZzQ7Ftxx1W8?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=218236420)
At the same time, Bellows revealed yet another lapse in election security.
"[O]ur elections division was notified by a private organization that they believed that they were in possession of absentee return envelopes for Maine. This was an out-of-state private organization," Bellows said.
She declined to name the organization and never said how that organization managed to come into possession of sensitive election materials.
Bellows subsequently said she'd referred the case to the FBI, yet the FBI also conducted no interviews with Newburgh officials concerning the event. Later, Bellows said the matter was being handled by Attorney General Aaron Frey, but no one from the AG's office has interviewed the resident who received the ballots or any Newburgh officials, and Frey has not made any announcements about how the chain of custody for sensitive election materials was broken in such an egregious fashion.
Months later, at a January hearing of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, Bellows again remained cagey about the identity of the DC-area group that somehow obtained election materials. Neither Bellows nor Deputy Secretary of State Julie Flynn could recall the name of the organization.
Once again, in response to direct emailed questions from lawmakers reviewed by the Maine Wire, Bellows and the Secretary of State's office refused to name the organization.
Yesterday evening, after multiple follow-up emails and several public posts questioning the lack of transparency from the Secretary of State, the office finally revealed that the contractor who obtained sensitive election materials in advance of the 2025 election was a left-wing non-profit with extensive pre-existing ties to Bellows.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..yTbNsOrBWrFzPH-RhdDrpbPfgpy0ijcVZzQ7Ftxx1W8?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=218236420)
"The company that received the one package of absentee envelopes is the Center for Civic Design," an anonymous Secretary of State office employee said in an email Monday.
Rep. David Boyer (R-Poland), the Republican lead on the VLA Committee who questioned Bellows about the envelopes in Maryland, was similarly stonewalled when he inquired privately about the identity of the political organization that somehow came into possession of sensitive election materials.
"Mainers were told these envelopes went to 'a private organization out of state.' Now we learn it was the Center for Civic Design -- a group with a long history with Secretary Bellows," Boyer told the Maine Wire.
"Official election materials don't belong in the hands of an outside advocacy group, and the Secretary owes the public a full accounting: who authorized this, how many envelopes, when, and why it took this long to name the recipient," said Boyer. "I have officially requested all correspondence between the Secretary of State's office and the Center for Civic Design."
"Transparency isn't optional when it comes to our elections," he said.

## The Center for Civic Design
The Center for Civic Design is an election-design nonprofit with longstanding connections to Maine's election administration, direct ties to Sec. Bellows and Democratic-aligned organizations.
The Center for Civic Design (CCD) is a Maryland 501(c)(3) that is almost entirely philanthropy-funded. Its board and money sit inside the same left-of-center election stack that includes [Center for Tech and Civic Life](https://substack.com/redirect/e9fa40d1-2bc6-407d-9028-24186fe001be?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), New Venture Fund / Hopewell / Civic (Re)Solve, the Institute for Responsive Government, [Center for Secure and Modern Elections](https://substack.com/redirect/6445ceb3-2263-4706-b772-e7d6545ec669?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), Democracy Fund, and Brennan Center.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2246936&post_id=218236420&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjE4MjM2NDIwLCJpYXQiOjE3OTA4MDI5ODMsImV4cCI6MTc5MzM5NDk4MywiaXNzIjoicHViLTIyNDY5MzYiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.M7M-KHKAht_F_asrpMF46RcOOTqZ50Bo3KlDFHkuEgM)
The purpose of CCD is to use private money from left-wing donors to shape the ballots and election processes that voters eventually use on Election Day.
In 2019, Bellows -- then a state lawmaker from Kennebec County -- was a cosponsor of LD 1463, a bill to establish automatic voter registration. The bill was introduced by then-House Speaker Sara Gideon (D-Freeport). That legislation was shaped, in part, through CCD's advocacy.
As secretary of state, Bellows later implemented automatic voter registration. CCD's 2022 annual report says the group tested Maine's automatic-registration materials with 32 participants in Augusta before the system's launch.
CCD also lists Maine organizations among its community partners, including AARP and Bernstein Shur. Other CCD partners in Maine include explicitly left-wing organizations that actively work to oppose Republican candidates for office and elect Democratic candidates for office, including Democracy Maine, the League of Women Voters of Maine and Maine Trans Net.
Another connection is Kathy Boockvar, CCD's vice chair and a former Pennsylvania secretary of state.
In December 2025, Boockvar joined a bipartisan group of former secretaries of state in a court filing supporting Bellows in a federal voter-roll lawsuit.
CCD's funding records show substantial support from nonprofit grantmakers, including the funds backed by George Soros and administered by the Arabella Advisers network.
[Share The Robinson Report](https://substack..GkX2s-vrCEKTO0ZEU-C7L0RnbMyOu6pOGVM6eRMV5bU?)
New Venture Fund tax filings report grants of $138,000 to CCD in each of 2020, 2021 and 2022. The Democracy Fund's 2023 tax return reports a $150,000 grant, and the MacArthur Foundation's 2024 return reports $500,000 in general operating support.
CCD's president, Sean Wang, has held leadership roles at Arabella.
CCD did not immediately respond to a phone call.
The Maine Wire submitted an additional Freedom of Access Act request to the Secretary of State on Wednesday in an attempt to glean more details as to how a left-wing NGO would have obtained sensitive election materials.
In addition, we asked the following question of Bellows, which went unanswered by press time:
* Why did your office wait so long to reveal that CCD obtained election materials?
* How did CCD obtain these materials? Did someone in the SOS office send them? Who?
* Were these materials stolen or lawfully obtained? Are you concerned about potential violations of federal law?
* What was the ostensibly legitimate purpose for providing this group with election materials?
* Who else did the SOS provide with election materials? Why?

_UPDATE: Following the publication of this story, we asked Secretary Bellows for a full list of third parties the Secretary sends sensitive election materials. An anonymous email from the Secretary of State 's office alleged that the office does not send election materials to third parties. The office did not explain how, then, a third party obtained sensitive election materials. We've submitted an additional Freedom of Access Act request to get additional information on this matter, so the story will be updated in a year or two when Bellows gets around to complying with transparency laws._

Secretary of State Shenna Bellows has refused to identify the name of a DC-area NGO that received Maine absentee ballot affidavit envelopes. On Tuesday, her office finally complied with a FOAA. Sep 30 | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows has finally responded to a Feb. 13 Freedom of Access Act request -- 228 days after the simple inquiry was submitted -- revealing that a left-wing NGO funded by George Soros and Arabella Advisers somehow obtained Maine election materials in advance of the 2025 election. The Maine Wire submitted the Freedom of Access Act request after a Maine resident discovered 250 Maine absentee ballots haphazardly packed into an Amazon Prime package and a delivered to their Newburgh home. In the following days, Sec. Bellows promised that her office would investigate the "bad actors" responsible for the worst breach in state election security in three decades, but her detectives never interviewed multiple individuals who handled the ballots after they were discovered. Investigative journalism costs time and money. Please consider supporting The Robinson Report with a subscription. At the same time, Bellows revealed yet another lapse in election security. "[O]ur elections division was notified by a private organization that they believed that they were in possession of absentee return envelopes for Maine. This was an out-of-state private organization," Bellows said. She declined to name the organization and never said how that organization managed to come into possession of sensitive election materials. Bellows subsequently said she'd referred the case to the FBI, yet the FBI also conducted no interviews with Newburgh officials concerning the event. Later, Bellows said the matter was being handled by Attorney General Aaron Frey, but no one from the AG's office has interviewed the resident who received the ballots or any Newburgh officials, and Frey has not made any announcements about how the chain of custody for sensitive election materials was broken in such an egregious fashion. Months later, at a January hearing of the Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee, Bellows again remained cagey about the identity of the DC-area group that somehow obtained election materials. Neither Bellows nor Deputy Secretary of State Julie Flynn could recall the name of the organization. Once again, in response to direct emailed questions from lawmakers reviewed by the Maine Wire, Bellows and the Secretary of State's office refused to name the organization. Yesterday evening, after multiple follow-up emails and several public posts questioning the lack of transparency from the Secretary of State, the office finally revealed that the contractor who obtained sensitive election materials in advance of the 2025 election was a left-wing non-profit with extensive pre-existing ties to Bellows. "The company that received the one package of absentee envelopes is the Center for Civic Design," an anonymous Secretary of State office employee said in an email Monday. Rep. David Boyer (R-Poland), the Republican lead on the VLA Committee who questioned Bellows about the envelopes in Maryland, was similarly stonewalled when he inquired privately about the identity of the political organization that somehow came into possession of sensitive election materials. "Mainers were told these envelopes went to 'a private organization out of state.' Now we learn it was the Center for Civic Design -- a group with a long history with Secretary Bellows," Boyer told the Maine Wire. "Official election materials don't belong in the hands of an outside advocacy group, and the Secretary owes the public a full accounting: who authorized this, how many envelopes, when, and why it took this long to name the recipient," said Boyer. "I have officially requested all correspondence between the Secretary of State's office and the Center for Civic Design." "Transparency isn't optional when it comes to our elections," he said. The Center for Civic Design The Center for Civic Design is an election-design nonprofit with longstanding connections to Maine's election administration, direct ties to Sec. Bellows and Democratic-aligned organizations. The Center for Civic Design (CCD) is a Maryland 501(c)(3) that is almost entirely philanthropy-funded. Its board and money sit inside the same left-of-center election stack that includes , New Venture Fund / Hopewell / Civic (Re)Solve, the Institute for Responsive Government, , Democracy Fund, and Brennan Center. The purpose of CCD is to use private money from left-wing donors to shape the ballots and election processes that voters eventually use on Election Day. In 2019, Bellows -- then a state lawmaker from Kennebec County -- was a cosponsor of LD 1463, a bill to establish automatic voter registration. The bill was introduced by then-House Speaker Sara Gideon (D-Freeport). That legislation was shaped, in part, through CCD's advocacy. As secretary of state, Bellows later implemented automatic voter registration. CCD's 2022 annual report says the group tested Maine's automatic-registration materials with 32 participants in Augusta before the system's launch. CCD also lists Maine organizations among its community partners, including AARP and Bernstein Shur. Other CCD partners in Maine include explicitly left-wing organizations that actively work to oppose Republican candidates for office and elect Democratic candidates for office, including Democracy Maine, the League of Women Voters of Maine and Maine Trans Net. Another connection is Kathy Boockvar, CCD's vice chair and a former Pennsylvania secretary of state. In December 2025, Boockvar joined a bipartisan group of former secretaries of state in a court filing supporting Bellows in a federal voter-roll lawsuit. CCD's funding records show substantial support from nonprofit grantmakers, including the funds backed by George Soros and administered by the Arabella Advisers network. ? New Venture Fund tax filings report grants of $138,000 to CCD in each of 2020, 2021 and 2022. The Democracy Fund's 2023 tax return reports a $150,000 grant, and the MacArthur Foundation's 2024 return reports $500,000 in general operating support. CCD's president, Sean Wang, has held leadership roles at Arabella. CCD did not immediately respond to a phone call. The Maine Wire submitted an additional Freedom of Access Act request to the Secretary of State on Wednesday in an attempt to glean more details as to how a left-wing NGO would have obtained sensitive election materials. In addition, we asked the following question of Bellows, which went unanswered by press time: Why did your office wait so long to reveal that CCD obtained election materials? How did CCD obtain these materials? Did someone in the SOS office send them? Who? Were these materials stolen or lawfully obtained? Are you concerned about potential violations of federal law? What was the ostensibly legitimate purpose for providing this group with election materials? Who else did the SOS provide with election materials? Why? UPDATE: Following the publication of this story, we asked Secretary Bellows for a full list of third parties the Secretary sends sensitive election materials. An anonymous email from the Secretary of State 's office alleged that the office does not send election materials to third parties. The office did not explain how, then, a third party obtained sensitive election materials. We've submitted an additional Freedom of Access Act request to get additional information on this matter, so the story will be updated in a year or two when Bellows gets around to complying with transparency laws. **Friend of Life,** When Isabella told the father of her baby she was pregnant, she was hoping for encouragement. Instead, she received a single text message. **"Abort."** Already grieving the loss of her toddler's father to cancer, Isabella suddenly found herself carrying another child without the support she desperately needed. Fear quickly gave way to hopelessness, and she became convinced there was only one way out of the situation she was facing. Then something unexpected happened. Instead of making a permanent decision she could never take back, Isabella found her way to a PreBorn! Network Clinic, where she was welcomed with compassion and surrounded by people who cared about both her and her baby. They listened to her story, answered her questions, talked honestly about parenting and adoption, and shared the hope of Jesus Christ with her. As those conversations continued, our staff introduced Isabella to Cari and Christian, a couple who had spent years praying that God would bless them with the opportunity to adopt a little girl. Months later, when Isabella gave birth, she spent 80 precious hours holding her daughter before placing her into Cari and Christian's arms. Then she quietly said the words they will never forget: **"You are going to be parents to Liliana."** What Isabella didn't know was that Cari and Christian had already chosen that very name years earlier while praying for the daughter they hoped God would one day provide. Only God could write a story like that. Every day at PreBorn!, we meet women who believe their circumstances will define the rest of their lives. Time and again, God reminds us that His plans are often greater than anything we could imagine. Your generosity helps make those moments possible. A gift of **$28 helps provide one life-saving ultrasound** , giving another woman the opportunity to slow down, receive compassionate care, and hear that both she and her baby are deeply loved by Jesus Christ. And because of a generous matching challenge, **every gift made before September 30 will be MATCHED dollar for dollar, up to $100,000.** Will you help another woman discover that hope is never beyond God's reach?

I'm not above going through it again](https://substack.com/redirect/c528ff6f-2307-4d7b-ad59-2b7de6eb7174?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

And although this is a fight I can lose
The accused is an innocent man

[Chorus]
I am an innocent man
Oh, yes I am
An innocent man
-Billy Joel
Before John Eastman, there was Nick Shirley. This year, California's Democratic supermajority passed -- and Gavin Newsom signed -- what critics rightly named the "Stop Nick Shirley Act": AB 2624, a bill that wraps taxpayer-funded immigrant-services nonprofits in a legal force field, sealing the addresses of their staff from public records and, as watchdogs and even members of Congress warn, exposing journalists to legal liability for doing exactly what Shirley did -- knocking on the doors where the public money went. Shirley is the independent reporter with nearly two million YouTube subscribers whose December videos documenting empty daycare centers allegedly billing for children who never showed up forced a conversation nobody in government wanted to have; his reward was a statute with his name on it, and a lawsuit he's now forced to file against the state. California's answer to scrutiny wasn't an audit. It was a law. Understand that pattern, because it's older than the bill number -- when the questions get too close to the machine, the machine rewrites the rules to punish the questioner. The Stop Nick Shirley Act does to citizen journalists what the State Bar of California already did to its premier conservative legal scholar: John Eastman, disbarred for his legal opinions about the 2020 election, his license stripped by a disciplinary judge whose donations went to the other party, with no criminal charge and no court sanction anywhere in the file. They came for the lawyers first. The lawyers are already gone. Now they're codifying it for everyone else -- and that is the backdrop against which docket No. 26-336, Eastman v. State Bar of California, landed on the Supreme Court's doorstep on September 14. It is not merely an appeal. It is the last exit before the door closes...

Now they're codifying it for everyone else. | | | Sep 30| | | ∙| | Preview ---|---|--- | | | | | | | | | | | | I'm not above being cool for a while If you're cruel to me, I'll understand Some people run from a possible fight Some people figure they can never win And although this is a fight I can lose The accused is an innocent man [Chorus] I am an innocent man Oh, yes I am An innocent man -Billy Joel Before John Eastman, there was Nick Shirley. This year, California's Democratic supermajority passed -- and Gavin Newsom signed -- what critics rightly named the "Stop Nick Shirley Act": AB 2624, a bill that wraps taxpayer-funded immigrant-services nonprofits in a legal force field, sealing the addresses of their staff from public records and, as watchdogs and even members of Congress warn, exposing journalists to legal liability for doing exactly what Shirley did -- knocking on the doors where the public money went. Shirley is the independent reporter with nearly two million YouTube subscribers whose December videos documenting empty daycare centers allegedly billing for children who never showed up forced a conversation nobody in government wanted to have; his reward was a statute with his name on it, and a lawsuit he's now forced to file against the state. California's answer to scrutiny wasn't an audit. It was a law. Understand that pattern, because it's older than the bill number -- when the questions get too close to the machine, the machine rewrites the rules to punish the questioner. The Stop Nick Shirley Act does to citizen journalists what the State Bar of California already did to its premier conservative legal scholar: John Eastman, disbarred for his legal opinions about the 2020 election, his license stripped by a disciplinary judge whose donations went to the other party, with no criminal charge and no court sanction anywhere in the file. They came for the lawyers first. The lawyers are already gone. Now they're codifying it for everyone else -- and that is the backdrop against which docket No. 26-336, Eastman v. State Bar of California, landed on the Supreme Court's doorstep on September 14. It is not merely an appeal. It is the last exit before the door closes... ### **TALENT, SKILL & PRIDE ACROSS THE COWBOY STATE **
---
| Hi friends,Kelly and I covered a lot of ground in the beautiful fall weather last week, from art in Cody to airplanes built in Afton to economic progress in Wheatland. Every town has its own specialties and strengths that contribute to our state, and our talent isn’t limited to one area. Our Wyoming pride is evident, well-earned, and impressive. We’re seeing continued support for this campaign from friends and folks we’re meeting for the first time, and we are appreciative every day. Some bring their questions; others bring their prayers, and we welcome them both. We enjoy every handshake, and Kelly and I have especially enjoyed meeting and talking with all of the kids who represent our next generation.For instance, Kelly was proud to hand off her leadership seat on the Campbell County Wool Growers Auxiliary to Kim Fry, one of the young people she had previously in her 4-H club. Kelly said it made her heart happy. I think that says it pretty well.We finished the weekend with unmatched Pokes pride in Laramie during Homecoming, where the Wyoming spirit was as "fevered" as our Cowboys, who took the win. The world needs more Cowboys!Eric

| **CHEYENNE**
I visited Frontier Park for the Indian Relay Championship of Champions. More than 100 teams representing 15 tribal nations came to Cheyenne to race. The horsemanship, teamwork and tradition are something to see. Thanks to Sen. Ogden Driskill for the invitation.I also want to share congrats to Campbell County’s Bob Tarver on his induction to the Cowboy Hall of Fame and to Rhonda Sedgwick Stearns of Newcastle on receiving the Cowboy Spirit Award.

---
| | |
---
|
---
| | | | |
---
| **GILLETTE** Kelly wrapped up her time as president of the Campbell County Wool Growers Auxiliary today and shared some news that made her smile. Kim Fry is stepping in as president. Years ago, Kim was in Kelly’s 4-H Young Leader Club.“It makes my heart happy,” Kelly said. Makayla Riley, also pictured, another young leader from that club, is also an Auxiliary member.It’s great to see young leaders carrying our ag message forward.
---
|
---
| | | **JACKSON** While in Jackson last week, Kelly and I joined the welcome reception for visitors from Lienz, Austria, Jackson’s sister city. I was glad to offer a few remarks and spend time with people who have kept this friendship going across the years.It was especially good to see Pepi Stiegler there. The Olympic gold-medal skier was born and raised in Lienz before moving to Jackson Hole, where he became the ski school director and helped put Jackson Hole Mountain Resort on the international map. Pepi’s connection to both communities helped spark the partnership between Jackson and Lienz.We also enjoyed visiting with Lienz historian Martin Kofler and Jackson local Becky Strout.
---
| | |
---
|
---
| | | **LINCOLN COUNTY**
Lincoln County kept us busy with stops in Star Valley Ranch, Afton, and Kemmerer.Kelly and I enjoyed visiting with folks at the meet-and-greet in Star Valley Ranch. At Star Valley Health in Afton, we had a good conversation about healthcare, property taxes, forest management, government efficiency, and civility. I appreciated former colleague Evan Simpson, Senator Dockstader, and Representative Erickson joining us.We also toured Aviat Aircraft on Afton’s Main Street. They build Husky planes flown around the world and Pitts aerobatic planes built to order. Seeing the work up close (some wings stitched by hand!) was something else.We wrapped up in Kemmerer with former colleagues Senator Baldwin and Representative Ember Oakley. Before we left, Laura, whose family owns the Place on Pine restaurant, caught us for a photo and told us she was excited to meet the next Governor. We hope she’s right! Either way, we’re grateful she came over to say hello.
---
| | |
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
|
---
| | | **STATEWIDE** I have been traveling around the state for over a year, showing up, listening and providing answers to questions voters want to know. The conversations are very much like Wyoming: direct, and not afraid to be tough. That’s how it should be.Along with many citizens, I’ve recently talked with radio station KHOL in Jackson, SVI Radio in Afton, and the Casper Star-Tribune. It’s important to get our message out to those who may not be able to attend an event, and we appreciate those in the media community who participate in the process. The regional blog Open Range Record came to our meet and greet today, and we chatted with them too. Leadership is about communicating clearly, widely and with respect. We’ll continue to do that up to November and beyond.
---
| | |
---
|
---
| | | | |
---
| **JACKSON** Kelly and I enjoyed celebrating Mary Martin’s retirement after more than 50 years of service with UW Extension in Teton County.Mary’s dedication has made a lasting difference for generations of Wyoming families and communities. It was great to spend time with those who gathered to recognize her remarkable career and thank her for the many years she has given to Teton County.Congratulations, Mary, and thank you for a lifetime of service to Wyoming!
---
|
---
| | | | |
---
| **JACKSON** Kelly and I enjoyed spending a day in Jackson and visiting community nonprofits that serve families and young people across Teton County and neighboring communities.At One22, we learned more about its work as a resource center and food distribution hub. Teton Youth and Family Services shared how its prevention, intervention, and postvention programs provide year-round support, with additional services during the summer. Through strong community partnerships, young people can quickly access therapists, crisis housing, stabilization services and other care before court intervention becomes necessary.We also visited the Community Foundation of Jackson Hole, which brings nonprofits and volunteer organizations together while providing financial assistance and space to collaborate. Kelly appreciated the opportunity to share her initiative SITE - Service In The Everyday - and the importance of connecting people with ways to serve their communities.Kelly and I also enjoyed a meet and greet at Phil Baux Park in Jackson. It was wonderful to meet with people of the community, and answer more of your questions!Thank you to everyone who took time to share their work with us
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
|
---
| | | **CODY** Kelly and I were honored to attend the Patrons Ball at the Buffalo Bill Center of the West in Cody, and celebrate the museum’s western arts community.The museum has grown from Peg Coe’s vision of bringing people together and showing what Wyoming folks can do when we put our minds to it. Today, the board continues her legacy through a week of events that helps strengthen the museum, support its future and keep the arts visible across our state.Thank you to Steve and Dana Cranfill for the warm welcome before the event, and to Naoma Tate for hosting the closing brunch at her ranch. It was great to spend time with the people who continue to support the arts and help this Wyoming tradition thrive!!

subject: I like where we are but this isn’t a done deal.
